requirements.text: /spar challenges the foundations in proportion to the decision. It writes down the premises that the code, docs, tests and past decisions give it. It tests the premises the decision depends on and marks each one checked, contradicted or unverified. It names weaknesses, debt, and whether a refactor must come first.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R3. Owner revision 2, item 3.

requirements.text: Two fresh debaters, a fresh Claude subagent and GPT through T3 Code, get the same frame and criteria. In the blind opening, neither sees the other. The coordinator argues no side. It frames the decision, checks objections and evidence, compares, and records.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R4. DECISIONS D5. Owner revision 2, item 4.

requirements.text: Depth is quick (1), standard (3), deep (5), a number, or until-agreement. It counts the exchanges after the opening. The default is standard, saved as `spar.default_depth` in `~/.workflow-axa/settings.json` through settings.py. The command overrides it.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R5. DECISIONS D8. Owner revision 2, item 1.

requirements.text: A round makes progress only with new discriminating evidence, a reasoned resolution, or a revision that fixes a named weakness. One exchange without progress stops the debate as stalled, and a repeated objection without new grounds is not progress. Before the coordinator calls a round stalled, it looks for a targeted question to you that could unblock it, and asks that question. Evidence that nobody can get makes the point unverifiable and sends it to you. An open decision of yours pauses the debate that depends on it. You stop the debate in plain words, which also cancels running delegates, and a late result cannot restart it.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R6. DECISIONS D6, D10. Owner revision 2, item 2.

requirements.text: Agreement means that both debaters judged the same proposal version and closed its material objections with reasons. A switch to the other side's already reviewed proposal needs no extra round. A mix of both is a new version that both must review. Nobody forces consensus.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R7. FINDINGS S1 O1, S4 C4. Owner revision 2, items 4 and 6.

requirements.text: You are the third participant. The agent researches and checks objective technical questions and never asks you about them. When requirements, priorities, trade-offs or acceptable risk are unclear, grilling asks you instead of the models guessing. No question is asked when evidence already settles the point. Questions reopen when the debate finds a new unknown. After your answer, each side revises its position or says why the answer does not change it.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R8. DECISIONS D10. Owner revision 2, item 5.

requirements.text: GPT is reached through the real capability list of T3 Code and `delegate_task`, with a new task for each exchange and `task_cancel` on stop. When GPT is unavailable or the capability check fails, the coordinator says so and asks you how to proceed. It never substitutes another model by itself. A failed check is reported as a failure, never as "GPT absent". With no second agent at all, it reports that sparring is not available.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R9. DECISIONS D10, which replaces D2 and D7. Owner revision 2, item 7.

requirements.text: /spar works for any kind of decision: features, changes, bugs, architecture, refactoring, tooling and general technical choices. It works with or without a codebase or task.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R10. Owner revision 2, item 10.

requirements.text: The coordinator is neutral but active. It argues no side, but it checks the cited evidence of each objection itself before it marks the objection resolved. It challenges agreement that rests on no evidence, because two "agree" answers without reasons are not agreement. It sends the gap back as an objection.

Foundation checks sort every premise into a verified fact, an unverified assumption or a contradiction. Passing tests show behavior, not that the architecture is right. Where premises are weak, the result shows the evidence and the alternatives and recommends one. The alternatives are refactor first, investigate first, or build on it as is. When that choice changes scope or priorities, grilling asks you. /spar refactors nothing.
requirements.origin: PLAN.md Agreement R12. DECISIONS D9, D10.

requirements.text: Unresolved objections are never dismissed. Each one is either a technical disagreement, reported with both positions and their evidence, or a decision that belongs to you, asked through grilling.

The amount of research and foundation checking follows the complexity and risk of the decision, not the debate depth. A quick debate on a risky decision still gets a full foundation check. A deep debate on a simple decision adds no research that it does not need.

sections.title: Context and scope
sections.locator: PLAN.md Goal. FINDINGS.md E1, E5, E8 and Overlap
sections.text:
Today you hold planning discussions between Claude and GPT by hand. In the session of 2026-11-16, Claude drafted an approach and GPT-6 Astra critiqued it in rounds. Each round was a new brief with the previous findings, until both agreed. You were asked only the decisions, and a topic took 2 to 3 rounds (FINDINGS E8).

No skill in the package proposes an approach and debates alternatives between models. plan-review, interrogate and codebase-design critique a plan or judge seams (FINDINGS E5). The way to reach GPT exists: the T3 Code tool `delegate_task` (FINDINGS E1).

Your request asked for a reusable /spar skill that replaces the manual discussions with structured, evidence-based sparring. It must reuse existing skills, use at most 3 debate rounds by default, and never force consensus. It must never implement without approval, must work for any project and language, and must keep token use down.

This plan builds /spar and hands its result to /workflow for planning and approval.

sections.title: Goals
sections.text:
You can type `/spar <problem> [depth]` in both hosts. Only you can start it. The model never starts it by itself (R1, A1).

A fresh Claude and GPT write blind opening positions. Then they exchange objections for the chosen depth: quick 1, standard 3, deep 5, a number, or until-agreement. The default comes from your settings.json (R4, R5).

The debate ends with one named outcome and a result. The result names the recommended approach, its evidence, rejected alternatives, risks, foundation changes, unresolved objections, your decisions and who debated (R6, R7, step 7).

You are asked only what belongs to you: requirements, priorities, trade-offs or acceptable risk. Objective facts are researched instead (R8).

Inside a task, the result becomes the Approach part of the agreement, and /workflow continues with the HOW. Without a task, no files are written (R1, R10).

When GPT is not reachable, /spar tells you and asks how to proceed (R9).

Live runs show how a model follows the skill, in one real decision and in staged scenarios (A4, A5).

sections.title: Non-goals
sections.locator: PLAN.md Agreement, Not included, R1 and R12. offer-1.json exclusions. FINDINGS.md F1
sections.text:
/spar does not plan the HOW. Files, interfaces, tests, the plan and the approval stay with workflow-specify (R1).

/spar never implements and never refactors, even when it finds a weak foundation. It shows the evidence and the alternatives instead (R1, R12).

Sparring never starts automatically. The workflow may recommend /spar for high-stakes work, but it never runs it (D3).

No separate SPAR.md. The result lives in the agreement or in the conversation (D4).

No third judge model, no code or experiments run during a debate, and no prototypes.

No change to T3 Code.

The fix for the approval hook bug (FINDINGS F1) is not part of this plan. You asked for it, and it becomes a separate task (D12).

No version bump and no CHANGELOG entry in this task. The release is a separate step.

sections.title: Overview
sections.locator: PLAN.md Agreement, What happens (steps 1 to 8) and Changes to the package
sections.text:
/spar is one small skill with one reference file. `skills/spar/SKILL.md` holds the steps. `skills/spar/T3.md` holds the T3 Code parts: the capability check, the debater brief, the ledger format and cancel. The skill owns only the debate. It uses grilling, workflow-clarify step 1, codebase-design and domain-modeling for everything else (R2).

The coordinator is the model you talk to. It first frames the decision in one sentence, with 3 to 6 criteria, the depth and the two debaters. Then it checks the premises that the decision depends on. Each premise becomes a verified fact, an unverified assumption or a contradiction (R3, R12). The amount of checking follows the risk of the decision, not the depth (R13).

You are the third participant. If something only you can decide blocks the frame or the debate, the coordinator asks you through grilling. Objective facts are researched and never asked (R8).

In the blind opening, a fresh Claude subagent and GPT get the same brief and write one position each. Neither sees the other. Each position has a recommendation, the rejected alternatives, the foundation weaknesses and the strongest uncertainty (R4).

In each exchange, both debaters get the latest position of the other side and the objection ledger. The ledger lists objections with stable IDs, each one open, resolved, needs you, or unverifiable. Each debater returns its strongest objection with evidence, its replies and what it changed. The coordinator argues no side. It checks the cited evidence itself, challenges agreement without evidence, and writes one progress line per round (R11).

The debate ends with one outcome, and the first match wins: cancelled, unavailable or interrupted, target changed, needs you, agreed, stalled, limit reached. Agreed needs both debaters to judge the same proposal version (R7). Stalled comes only after the coordinator found no question to you that could unblock the round (R6). Real disagreement is reported and never forced into agreement (R14).

The result lists the recommended approach, its evidence and the rejected alternatives. It also lists risks, required foundation changes, unresolved objections, your decisions, who debated, whether it was cross-model, and the outcome. Inside a task, the rounds go to FINDINGS, your choices go to DECISIONS, and the result becomes the Approach part of the agreement (D4). Then workflow-clarify asks you to agree, and workflow-specify plans the HOW. Without a task, the result stays in the conversation.

If GPT is missing or the T3 Code capability check fails, the coordinator says so and asks you how to proceed. One option you can choose is a fresh helper of the same model, labelled "single model, fresh context, not cross-model" (R9). You can stop the debate in plain words at any time, which also cancels running delegates (R6).

The main trade-off is cost against independence. Each exchange launches two fresh debaters, so the coordinator does not anchor the debate. This doubles the model runs per round (D5, FINDINGS S4 C1).

sections.title: Alternatives considered
sections.locator: DECISIONS.md D1 to D12. FINDINGS.md Questions Q1 to Q9
sections.text:
D1: /spar is a new skill that you start, and it owns only the debate. It plugs into workflow-clarify. You chose it over an option inside workflow-clarify and over a standalone skill with its own document. It keeps one small skill for the only new part.

D3: Only you start /spar. The workflow may recommend it for high-stakes work but never runs it. You chose this over the workflow running it by itself, because each round costs model runs.

D4: The result goes into the agreement in PLAN.md as an Approach part, and the rounds go to FINDINGS. You chose this over a separate SPAR.md, so that there is one agreement and one approval.

D5: Two fresh debaters always run, a fresh Claude subagent and GPT. The coordinator only frames, compares and records. You chose this over the coordinator debating as the Claude side, which halves the runs but weakens independence.

D6: until-agreement has no pauses and no ceiling. It writes a progress line each round and stops on no progress, repeated arguments, missing evidence, an open decision of yours or your stop. You chose this over a pause every 5 rounds. A number as depth gives a budget when you want one.

D8: The blind opening always runs, and depth counts the exchanges after it. The default is standard, saved through settings.py, and the command overrides it without saving. You chose this over counting the opening as a round.

D2 and D7, superseded by D10: a missing GPT first led to an automatic fresh helper of the same model, with a label. D10 replaced this. Now the coordinator asks you how to proceed, and that helper is one option you can choose.

D9: You agreed agreement 2 with four additions. Your words said "three final adjustments" and then added a fourth about the tests (D12). The coordinator is neutral but active. Foundation checks separate facts, assumptions and contradictions. Research scales with risk, not with depth. Tests cover the failure cases, not only the happy path.

D10: You answered Q9 with neither option. /spar is an interactive sparring skill, not a decision engine, and you are the third participant. The tests check the decision process, not predetermined answers. Unclear priorities, trade-offs or risk go to you through grilling.

D11: You answered offer #1 (b0b0fa425dd9a16c) with "Approve from this summary", which also agreed to agreement 3. The report was recommended then and not chosen.

D12: After that approval, you asked to see the plan before the build ("also let me first see the plan before we build"). This report answers that request, and offer #1 is asked again, so the agent waits for your OK on it. You also asked for the hook bug F1 to be fixed ("That bug needs fixing"). It becomes a separate task.

sections.title: Cross-cutting concerns
sections.locator: FINDINGS.md S5, F1. TODO.md T4, T6
sections.text:
Live behavior is proven only in T6. Offline tests show that the skill text states each rule. They cannot show that a model follows it (FINDINGS S5).

The skill depends on how well a model follows its text. Debaters may still agree without evidence or repeat themselves. The checks of the coordinator (R11) and the T6 scenarios address this, but they observe behavior and do not guarantee it.

Cost: T6 can use up to 26 debater launches and 8 coordinator sessions. Each batch runs only after your OK right before it, and you may stop after any batch. No research agents run, and no retry happens without your OK. Subscription limits apply. Each normal /spar exchange also launches two debaters.

The approval hook has a bug (FINDINGS F1). An approval given with the button of the question tool does not lift an earlier "Do not implement until I approve that plan" pause. Every write is then refused until you type a continue. This offer excludes hooks, so the fix becomes a separate task that you asked for (D12).

The "capability check failed" case cannot be staged safely. It stays NOT VERIFIED unless it happens by itself (TODO T6).

sections.text:
Offline contract tests run in the normal suite. tests/test_spar.py pins one rule for each requirement, and tests/test_settings.py covers the depth setting. tests/test_owned_skills.py covers the new case of grilling. tools/validate.py must pass with 20 skills. Tests come first in T1 to T4.

Live process scenarios run only in ticket T6, in T3 Code, on disposable pilot projects outside every checkout. They stage situations such as unclear priorities, false consensus, stagnation, missing GPT and a questionable architecture. Each one is recorded as observed, not provoked, or failed. No scenario prescribes the recommended answer (A5, D10).

GPT-6 Astra and a fresh Opus review the skill text until both agree. At the end the full suite runs with `python -X utf8 -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py"`.

tickets.specification:
Create `skills/spar/SKILL.md` with `disable-model-invocation: true`. It runs the eight steps of agreement 3: frame, foundations, owner questions, blind opening, exchanges, end, result and handoff. It reads the bundled skills by path and names `research` and `diagnosing-bugs` only as optional external specialists. It copies none of their rules.

`skills/spar/T3.md` holds the capability check and its three answers, the debater brief, the ledger format, one new task per exchange, and `task_cancel` on stop. /spar reads it on every run. `skills/spar/agents/openai.yaml` sets `allow_implicit_invocation: false`, and `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` registers `./skills/spar`.

SPECIALISTS.md gets a /spar row: started by you, recommended for high-stakes choices, never run by the workflow. Step 3 of workflow-clarify accepts an optional Approach part from /spar. CONTEXT.md gets the term "Spar", and docs/RULE-CONTRACTS.md gets a /spar row. The current skill count goes from 19 to 20. The hooks, the offer model, workflow-specify, plan-review and interrogate do not change.
tickets.expected: tests/test_spar.py holds one contract check for each requirement, written before the skill. GPT-6 Astra and a fresh Opus review the skill text until both agree.

tickets.specification:
Write `tests/behavioral/spar.json`. Every scenario has `mode: live-host` and `result: NOT_RUN` until it is observed. Each scenario has a staged situation, the process checks to observe, and an explicit "no prescribed answer". The scenarios cover unclear priorities, a disputed objective fact, false consensus, stagnation and unresolved objections. They also cover missing GPT, a questionable existing architecture, no codebase or task, and cancel during a run.

A test in tests/test_spar.py reads the file. It looks for every scenario, for no prescribed answer, and for each named rule in the skill text. This is authored coverage only. Nothing here counts as observed behavior.
tickets.expected: False consensus: "agreed" is reported only after the gap is closed with evidence. Otherwise the gap stays an open objection under another outcome. Stagnation: the coordinator first looks for a question to you that could unblock the debate. It reports "stalled" with both positions only when no such question exists.

tickets.specification: README lists /spar with the other user commands and says 20 skills. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md places /spar before the agreement of workflow-clarify (WHAT and WHY) and workflow-specify after it (HOW). tests/README.md names tests/test_spar.py and tests/behavioral/spar.json and says that the scenarios are live-only. The CHANGELOG entry is written at release, not here.
tickets.expected: tools/validate.py passes its count and link checks, and the full suite passes.

tickets.specification:
The agent builds a ZIP of the candidate with tools/build_release.py. For each run, a new project under D:/workflow-axa-spar-pilot/<run>/ gets the 20 skill folders in `.claude/skills/`, and a T3 Code thread opened on it loads them. Each run records the snapshot id of the source worktree. It also records the transcript line that shows /spar loaded from that project, not from the installed plugin.

Run 1 is a real decision that you pick, at quick depth. Runs 2 to 6 stage unclear priorities, a disputed fact outside any task, and false consensus. They also stage stagnation at standard depth and questionable architecture on a small sample repository. Run 7 is missing GPT in a Claude Code CLI session, and run 8 is a cancel during run 2.

The total cap is 26 debater launches and 8 coordinator sessions. No research agents run, and no retry happens without your OK. Each batch runs only after your OK right before it. The pilot folders are removed after the evidence is recorded, except a run kept as evidence of a failure.
tickets.expected: Each scenario is recorded against its own T4 process checks as observed (with the quote), not provoked, or failed. The "capability check failed" case cannot be staged safely and stays NOT VERIFIED unless it happens by itself.
